body: Lithuanian licence plates are long and white, with the standard blue European strip on the left.
Lithuanian bollards are wedge-shaped with a rectangular orange reflector on the front and a white reflector on the back. A thinner version also exists.
Lithuanian poles are usually square and concrete, and often feature a diagonal support beam. While most common in Lithuania, they can also be found in Estonia and rarely in Latvia.

Typical Lithuanian poletops often have short horizontal rods for insulators. Some arrange the insulators in a trident-like shape. These poletops are not unique and can be found in other post-Soviet countries.
Lithuania uses white chevrons with red arrows. Small single chevrons often have a red outline. This color scheme helps distinguish it from Estonia, Russia, and Ukraine, which use the opposite.
While all Baltic countries use a blue kilometre marker, Lithuania's is set at a 45° angle to the road. The sign itself has an L-shape.
Lithuanian warning and speed signs have a relatively thin red border with a thin white outline.
Lithuania uses standard A-type guardrails with orange reflectors. This distinguishes them from Estonia (no reflectors) and Latvia (red or white reflectors).
Lithuanian pedestrian signs have 3 stripes and a pedestrian shape with a low level of detail. This design is shared with Russia and Ukraine.
Lithuanian bus stop signs show a bus with four windows. This distinguishes them from Latvian signs (five windows), but they are identical to Estonian signs.
The Lithuanian language is a Baltic language. Look for unique letters with hooks (Ą, Ę, Į, Ų), an Ė with a dot, and the letter Y.
The Lithuanian word for street is 'gatvė', often abbreviated as 'g.' on signs. This word is almost entirely unique to Lithuania.
Many Lithuanian place names end in -ai.
Lithuanian architecture features light-coloured brick buildings with steep corrugated metal roofs. Wooden buildings and pastel-painted stone buildings are also common.
Lithuanian directional signs are blue with white text. The arrowhead has a vertical back, which distinguishes it from the more stylized arrow on Latvian signs.
Lithuania has less forest cover than the other two Baltic countries, resulting in a more open and agricultural landscape, though this can vary.
Generation 3 coverage in Lithuania often has random small blurs, frequently on directional signs. This meta is shared with Kaliningrad but not Estonia or Latvia.
Lithuania is mostly flat, but its hilliest areas are in the southeast and the central-western part of the country.
The Curonian Spit south of Klaipeda features road 167, a north-south road with Generation 4 coverage through a forest of often windswept Baltic pines.
On the Curonian Spit, you can find wooden and often red Scandinavian-style houses.
Rarely, you can see bilingual signs with the Polish language in a small area of southeastern Lithuania.
